title: Add Months to a Date — addMonths
text: Naively adding months date can produce invalid results. example, adding one month .Date("2013-01-31") returns "2013-02-28" rather date March. arguments x n recycled common maximum length using bedrock::recycle(). Partial recycling produce warning. either argument length zero, empty Date vector returned. Missing values either argument produce missing values corresponding result. Inputs supplied POSIXct converted Date, time--day information discarded. default, .Date.POSIXct performs conversion UTC. Supply tz ... another time zone determine calendar date.

title: Add Months to a Date — addMonths
code: # character input is converted to Date addMonths("2013-01-31", 1) #> [1] "2013-02-28"  # negative values subtract months addMonths(as.Date("2013-03-31"), -1) #> [1] "2013-02-28"  # x and n are recycled addMonths(   c("2013-01-31", "2013-03-31", "2013-10-31", "2013-12-31"),   c(1, -1) ) #> [1] "2013-02-28" "2013-02-28" "2013-11-30" "2013-11-30"  # missing values propagate addMonths(c("2013-01-31", NA), 1) #> [1] "2013-02-28" NA            # POSIXct input is converted to Date x <- as.POSIXct(c("2015-01-31", "2015-08-31"), tz = "UTC") addMonths(x, c(1, 3), tz = "UTC") #> [1] "2015-02-28" "2015-11-30"  # numeric dates require an origin x <- as.numeric(as.Date(c("2015-01-31", "2015-08-31"))) addMonths(x, c(1, 3), origin = as.Date("1970-01-01")) #> [1] "2015-02-28" "2015-11-30"

Examples: plotQQ(x), plotECDF(x), plotCor(x, method = "spearman")

title: Atkinson Index — atkinson
text: frequency weights \(n_i\), weighted arithmetic mean $$ \bar{x}_n = \frac{\sum_i n_i x_i}{\sum_i n_i}. $$ \(\varepsilon \ne 1\), Atkinson index $$ (\varepsilon) = 1 - \frac{ \left( \frac{\sum_i n_i x_i^{1-\varepsilon}}      {\sum_i n_i} \right)^{1/(1-\varepsilon)} }{\bar{x}_n}. $$ \(\varepsilon = 1\), $$ (1) = 1 - \frac{ \exp\left( \frac{\sum_i n_i \log(x_i)}      {\sum_i n_i} \right) }{\bar{x}_n}. $$ calculation uses normalized frequency weights logarithmic power means. therefore construct potentially large vector result rep(x, n). Observations zero frequency ignored. frequencies zero observations remain removing missing values, NA_real_ returned. values zero, index defined zero. least one value zero epsilon >= 1, equally distributed equivalent value zero index one. Negative values, non-finite values, missing values na.rm = FALSE produce NA_real_. negative epsilon also produces NA_real_.

title: Box-Cox Transformation — boxCox
text: Box-Cox transformation defined strictly positive values x given $$ f_\lambda(x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}   (x^\lambda - 1) / \lambda & \mbox{} \lambda \neq 0 \\   \log(x)                   & \mbox{} \lambda = 0 \end{array} \right. $$ transformation requires strictly positive input values. |lambda| < tol, logarithmic transformation used instead numerical stability. inverse transformation recovers original data (numerical precision) lambda tol used.

text: order coefficient variation unbiased estimate true population value, coefficient variation corrected : $$ CV_{korr} = CV \cdot \left( 1 - \frac{1}{4\cdot(n-1)} + \frac{1}{n} \cdot CV^2 + \frac{1}{2 \cdot (n-1)^2} \right) $$ determining confidence intervals  coefficient variation number methods proposed. coefVarCI() currently supports four different methods. details methods given specific references. "naive" method   based dividing standard confidence limit standard deviation sample mean. McKay's   approximation asymptotically exact n goes infinity. McKay recommends approximation coefficient variation less 0.33. Note coefficient variation greater 0.33, either normality data suspect probability negative values data non-negligible. case, McKay's approximation may valid. Also, generally recommended sample size least 10 using McKay's approximation. Vangel's modified McKay method   accurate McKay method cases, particularly small samples. According Vangel, unmodified McKay accurate coefficient variation alpha large. However, coefficient variation large, implies either data contains negative values data follow normal distribution. case, neither McKay modified McKay used. general, Vangel's modified McKay method recommended McKay method. generally provides good approximations long data approximately normal coefficient variation less 0.33. See also: https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/software/dataplot/refman1/auxillar/coefvacl.htm nct  uses noncentral t-distribution calculate confidence intervals. See Smithson (2003). sides names side finite bound lies: "left" yields \([lci, \infty)\), "right" yields \((-\infty, uci]\). text: Pearson's contingency coefficient ranges 0 \(\sqrt{(m-1)/m}\), \(m = \min(r, c)\). Consequently, attainable maximum depends dimensions table. Since generally accepted analytical interval available, bootstrap intervals implemented. interval obtained multinomial bootstrap cells table. Two arguments configure , passed ...: R, number replicates (default 999), type, one "perc" (default) "bca". "bca" better choice tables clearly non-zero association reasonable number observations. Confidence intervals restricted attainable range. run the ANOVA summary(anova1)                                      # print the ANOVA table #>             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)   #> treatment1   2  7.936   3.968   3.663 0.0913 . #> Residuals    6  6.500   1.083                  #> --- #> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1 etaSq(anova1)                                        # effect size #>               eta.sq eta.sq.part #> treatment1 0.5497229   0.5497229  #### Example 2: two-way ANOVA ####  treatment2 <- factor(c(1,2,3,1,2,3,1,2,3))       # second grouping variable anova2 <- aov(outcome ~ treatment1 + treatment2) # run the ANOVA summary(anova2)                                  # print the ANOVA table #>             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value  Pr(>F)    #> treatment1   2  7.936   3.968    55.8 0.00120 ** #> treatment2   2  6.216   3.108    43.7 0.00191 ** #> Residuals    4  0.284   0.071                    #> --- #> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1 etaSq(anova2)                                    # effect size #>               eta.sq eta.sq.part #> treatment1 0.5497229   0.9653961 #> treatment2 0.4305727   0.9562393  #### Example 3: two-way ANOVA unbalanced cell sizes #### #### data from Maxwell & Delaney, 2004              #### #### Designing experiments and analyzing data       ####  dfMD <- data.frame(IV1=factor(rep(1:3, c(3+5+7, 5+6+4, 5+4+6))),                    IV2=factor(rep(rep(1:3, 3), c(3,5,7, 5,6,4, 5,4,6))),                    DV=c(c(41, 43, 50), c(51, 43, 53, 54, 46), c(45, 55, 56, 60, 58, 62, 62),                         c(56, 47, 45, 46, 49), c(58, 54, 49, 61, 52, 62), c(59, 55, 68, 63),                         c(43, 56, 48, 46, 47), c(59, 46, 58, 54), c(55, 69, 63, 56, 62, 67)))  # use contr.sum for correct sum of squares type 3 dfMD$IV1s <- C(dfMD$IV1, "contr.sum") dfMD$IV2s <- C(dfMD$IV2, "contr.sum") dfMD$IV1t <- C(dfMD$IV1, "contr.treatment") dfMD$IV2t <- C(dfMD$IV2, "contr.treatment")  etaSq(aov(DV ~ IV1s*IV2s, data=dfMD), type=3) #>                eta.sq eta.sq.part #> IV1s      0.086255016  0.16919863 #> IV2s      0.497535493  0.54017354 #> IV1s:IV2s 0.005976273  0.01391427 etaSq(aov(DV ~ IV1t*IV2t, data=dfMD), type=1) #>                eta.sq eta.sq.part #> IV1t      0.042592627  0.09137634 #> IV2t      0.527900579  0.55484898 #> IV1t:IV2t 0.005976273  0.01391427  #### Example 4: two-way split-plot ANOVA -> etaSq.aovlist ####  set.seed(1) DV_t1 <- round(rnorm(3*10, -0.5, 1), 2) DV_t2 <- round(rnorm(3*10,  0,   1), 2) DV_t3 <- round(rnorm(3*10,  0.5, 1), 2) dfSPF <- data.frame(id=factor(rep(1:(3*10), times=3)),                     IVbtw=factor(rep(LETTERS[1:3], times=3*10)),           IVwth=factor(rep(1:3, each=3*10)),           DV=c(DV_t1, DV_t2, DV_t3)) spf <- aov(DV ~ IVbtw*IVwth + Error(id/IVwth), data=dfSPF) etaSq(spf, type=1, anova=TRUE) #>                 eta.sq eta.sq.part eta.sq.gen         SS df        MS      SSE #> IVbtw       0.01359217  0.03775582 0.01693141  1.1645622  2 0.5822811 29.68002 #> IVwth       0.18569613  0.29547219 0.19048057 15.9102422  2 7.9551211 37.93659 #> IVbtw:IVwth 0.01152556  0.02536984 0.01439415  0.9874978  4 0.2468744 37.93659 #>             dfE          F            p #> IVbtw        27  0.5297029 5.947733e-01 #> IVwth        54 11.3235402 7.820776e-05 #> IVbtw:IVwth  54  0.3514079 8.419225e-01

title: Safe (Generalized) Huber M-Estimator of Location — huberM
text: Wald interval (method = "wald") Uses empirical sandwich standard error Huber M-estimator: $$   \hat\mu \;\pm\; t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}   \hat s \sqrt{\frac{\hat\tau}{n}}, $$ $$   \hat\tau =   \frac{n \sum_{=1}^n \psi_k(r_i)^2}        {\left\{\sum_{=1}^n (|r_i| \leq k)\right\}^2},   \qquad   r_i = \frac{x_i-\hat\mu}{\hat s}. $$ , \(\psi_k\) denotes Huber score function. additional small-sample adjustment applied beyond use t-quantile. Bootstrap interval (method = "boot") statistic \(\hat\mu\) resampled \(R\) times.  Note mu s fixed initial values (computed full data resampling) re-estimated resample.  bootstrap therefore targets variability location estimator fixed scale initialization, fully re-estimated robust estimator.  Bootstrap arguments passed ... extracted via .extractBootArgs(): R number bootstrap replicates (default 999) type confidence interval type: "perc" "bca" (default) parallel parallelization mode: "", "multicore", "snow" (default "") ncpus number CPUs parallel bootstrap (default getOption("boot.ncpus", 1L)) original internal estimator accessible DescToolsX:::.huberM.

text: ICC measure reliability ratings \(n\) subjects \(k\) raters. specific coefficient depends three design decisions: model: one-way two-way ANOVA design type: agreement consistency unit: single rating average k ratings six classical Shrout–Fleiss cases : model = "oneway" type = "agreement" meaningful. Confidence intervals can computed using different inference methods: "anova": exact F-based intervals following Shrout Fleiss (1979) "reml": variance components estimated via REML. Point estimate ; confidence interval available method. "boot": nonparametric percentile bootstrap ICC(1) based one-way random effects ANOVA measures absolute agreement. ICC(2) assumes raters randomly sampled generalizable, ICC(3) assumes fixed set raters. average forms (k) reflect reliability mean k raters correspond Spearman–Brown adjusted reliability. ANOVA-based confidence intervals follow exact formulas Shrout Fleiss (1979), including variance approximation ICC(2).

title: Kappa for m Raters — kappaM
text: three coefficients contrast mean observed agreement agreement expected chance, differ chance agreement derived. "fleiss" Fleiss (1971) bases chance agreement category proportions pooled across raters. generalises Scott's pi (Scott, 1955), \(m = 2\) equals Scott's pi - Cohen's kappa. "conger" Conger (1980) derives chance agreement rater's marginal distribution, reduces exactly Cohen's kappa \(m = 2\). "light" Light (1971) unweighted mean \(\binom{m}{2}\) pairwise Cohen kappas. Confidence intervals Wald type. "fleiss" "conger" standard error analytic one given respective author. "light" closed-form variance exists; since estimate mean pairwise kappas, standard error estimated standard deviation divided \(\sqrt{\binom{m}{2}}\). treats pairwise kappas independent, - share raters - interval approximate tends narrow. bootstrap interval preferable assumption doubtful. Kappa lies \([-1, 1]\), interval restricted range open side one-sided interval reported boundary rather \(\pm\infty\). See ConfidenceIntervals.

title: Ordinal Association Measures — ordAssocs
text: Let \(P\) \(Q\) denote numbers concordant discordant pairs, \(T_X\) \(T_Y\) numbers tied \(X\) \(Y\), \(n_0=n(n-1)/2\), \(m\) smaller table dimension. conDisPairs returns pair counts C, D, Ties_X, Ties_Y describes calculation. measures defined follows: Goodman–Kruskal \(\gamma\) (gkGamma): $$\gamma = \frac{P-Q}{P+Q}$$ Kendall \(\tau_a\) (kendallTauA): $$\tau_a = \frac{P-Q}{n_0}$$ Kendall \(\tau_b\) (kendallTauB): $$       \tau_b =       \frac{P-Q}       {\sqrt{(n_0-T_X)(n_0-T_Y)}}     $$ Stuart \(\tau_c\) (stuartTauC): $$       \tau_c =       \frac{2m(P-Q)}       {n^2(m-1)}     $$ Somers \(D_{X\mid Y}\) (somersDelta): $$       D_{X\mid Y} =       \frac{P-Q}       {n_0-T_Y}     $$ Gamma Kendall's coefficients symmetric. Somers' \(D\) directional: tables, direction="row" returns \(D_{R|C}\) direction="column" returns \(D_{C|R}\). vector mode, ordAssocs() returns \(D_{X|Y}\); reverse x y direction. somersDelta() performs reversal direction="column". c-statistic used binary outcome consistently ordered predictions related Somers D \(C_{stat}=(D+1)/2\). title: Randolph's Free-Marginal Multirater Kappa — randolphKappa
text: Let \(k\) number categories, \(m\) number raters, \(N\) number subjects. Randolph's kappa $$\kappa = \frac{P_o - 1/k}{1 - 1/k},$$ observed agreement \(P_o\) proportion agreeing rater pairs, $$P_o = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{=1}^{N}       \frac{\sum_{j} n_{ij}(n_{ij}-1)}{m(m-1)}.$$ , \(n_{ij}\) denotes number raters assigned subject \(\) category \(j\). observed agreement Fleiss' kappa (computed percAgreement); Randolph's coefficient differs Fleiss' chance agreement \(P_e\), fixed \(1/k\) instead estimated marginals. \(P_e = 1/k\) refers categories rater chosen, happen occur data. category available never used, default categories = NULL understates \(k\) thus overstates chance agreement, biases \(\kappa\) downwards. Supply categories whenever coding scheme known. Long-format ratings can first reshaped raterFrame.

title: Simpson Diversity Indices — simpson
text: Gini-Simpson index defined \(1 - \sum p_i^2\), \(p_i\) relative frequencies categories. Hunter-Gaston index defined \(1 - \sum n_i (n_i - 1) / (N (N - 1))\), \(n_i\) counts \(N\) total sample size. Deltas correction defined \((1 - \sum p_i^2) * k / (k - 1)\), \(k\) number observed (non-empty) categories. factor reciprocal \((k-1)/k\), largest value Gini-Simpson index can attain \(k\) categories, corrected index reaches 1 uniform distribution observed categories. indices represent probability two randomly selected observations belong different categories. Hunter-Gaston index corrects finite sample size, Deltas correction adjusts small number observed categories. Note finite-sample correction \(N/(N-1)\) applied Gini-Simpson index reproduces Hunter-Gaston index exactly; two adjustment \(N\) \(k\) correction factor. sample concentrated single category perfectly homogeneous rather undefined, "gini" "hunter" return 0 . Deltas correction requires \(k \ge 2\), since \(k - 1\) appears denominator. x numeric, treated vector counts. Non-integer values produce warning; Hunter-Gaston index requires integer counts.

Review Economics Statistics, 85(1), 226-234. https://doi.org/10.1162/rest.2003.85.1.226

title: Tschuprow's T — tschuprowT

title: Tschuprow's T — tschuprowT
text: numeric scalar containing Tschuprow's T

title: Tschuprow's T — tschuprowT
text: y provided, contingency table created using table(x, y, ...). Otherwise, x assumed already two-dimensional contingency table. Tschuprow's T defined : $$ T = \sqrt{ \frac{\chi^2}{n \sqrt{(r - 1)(c - 1)}} } $$ \(\chi^2\) chi-squared statistic, \(n\) total sample size, \(r\) \(c\) number rows columns contingency table. correct = TRUE, bias-corrected version computed based Bergsma (2013), adjusts estimate especially small samples. replaces \(\phi^2 = \chi^2/n\) \(\tilde\phi^2 = \max(0, \phi^2 - (r-1)(c-1)/(n-1))\) dimensions \(\tilde r = r - (r-1)^2/(n-1)\) \(\tilde c = c - (c-1)^2/(n-1)\). 2x2 table T coincides Cramer's V absolute value phi coefficient; sign association reported.

title: Tschuprow's T — tschuprowT
text: Tschuprow, . . (1939). Principles Mathematical Theory Correlation. W. Hodge & Co. Bergsma, W. (2013). bias-correction Cramer's V Tschuprow's T. Journal Korean Statistical Society, 42(3), 323–328. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jkss.2012.10.002

title: Tschuprow's T — tschuprowT
code: # Example with vectors x <- c("A", "A", "B", "B") y <- c("yes", "no", "yes", "no") tschuprowT(x, y) #> [1] 0  # Example with contingency table tab <- matrix(c(10, 20, 30, 40), nrow = 2) tschuprowT(tab)               # 0.08908708 #> [1] 0.08908708  # Bias-corrected version: the correction exceeds the estimate here, # so the corrected value is 0 tschuprowT(tab, correct = TRUE) #> [1] 0

title: Yeo-Johnson Transformation — yeoJohnson

title: Yeo-Johnson Transformation — yeoJohnson
text: Yeo-Johnson transformation extends Box-Cox transformation allow zero negative values. defined piecewise: $$f_\lambda(x) = \frac{(x+1)^\lambda - 1}{\lambda}$$ \(x \ge 0\) \(\lambda \ne 0\), $$f_\lambda(x) = \log(x+1)$$ \(x \ge 0\) \(\lambda = 0\), $$f_\lambda(x) = -\frac{(-x+1)^{2-\lambda} - 1}{2-\lambda}$$ \(x < 0\) \(\lambda \ne 2\), $$f_\lambda(x) = -\log(-x+1)$$ \(x < 0\) \(\lambda = 2\). transformation defined real-valued inputs continuous differentiable \(x\). commonly used alternative Box-Cox transformation data include zero negative values. transformation strictly increasing maps 0 0, sign transformed value identifies branch inverted. inverse transformation recovers original data (numerical precision) lambda tol used. \(\lambda < 0\) image transformation bounded \(-1/\lambda\) (correspondingly \(\lambda > 2\) ); values outside range preimage reported error.

title: Yeo-Johnson Transformation — yeoJohnson
text: Yeo, .-K. Johnson, R. . (2000). new family power transformations improve normality symmetry. Biometrika, 87(4), 954–959.

title: Yeo-Johnson Transformation — yeoJohnson
code: set.seed(1) x <- rnorm(500)  y <- yeoJohnson(x, lambda = 0.5) x_back <- yeoJohnsonInv(y, lambda = 0.5)  # Check inversion max(abs(x - x_back)) #> [1] 1.332268e-15  # Compare with log-like transformation y0 <- yeoJohnson(x, lambda = 0)

title: Yule's Coefficients of Association (Q and Y) — yule
text: 2x2 table cell counts \(, b, c, d\): Odds ratio: $$= \frac{ad}{bc}$$ Yule's Q: $$Q = \frac{- 1}{+ 1}      = \tanh\left(\frac{1}{2}\log()\right)$$ Yule's Y: $$Y = \frac{\sqrt{} - 1}{\sqrt{} + 1}      = \tanh\left(\frac{1}{4}\log()\right)$$ coefficients computed tanh form, stays well defined zero cell drives odds ratio 0 Inf (coefficient -1 1). Confidence intervals obtained asymptotic normal approximation: $$\log() \pm z \cdot \sqrt{1/+ 1/b + 1/c + 1/d}$$ transformed selected coefficient. zero cell standard error infinite interval degenerates \([-1, 1]\); use correct = TRUE obtain finite interval. one-sided interval open side reported range limit (-1 resp. 1), \(\pm\infty\).
